definition: Extraneous means irrelevant, extra, not necessary.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word extraneous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know extraneous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Log only the pendulum's swing time, the lab sheet warns; the color of the string is extraneous data.
An unneeded detail merely fails to help; an extraneous one comes from outside the subject entirely — it was never part of the matter to begin with.
Distracting sits a rung past extraneous: the imported material has stopped being harmless and started pulling attention away from the point.

Irrelevant judges a thing against the question at hand: whatever it is and wherever it came from, it fails to bear on the point. Extraneous adds a story about origin — the material walked in from outside the subject entirely. A detail can be irrelevant while still belonging to the file; extraneous detail never belonged.

Unrelated is the total break: the thing has no connection to the matter at all, near or far. Extraneous is softer and more particular — extraneous material can touch the subject and still not belong, because it was imported from somewhere else. Everything unrelated is extraneous; not the reverse.

Charming, every one — and none of it had anything to do with volcanoes.
Extraneous is the precise word because the material comes from outside the subject.
The dog photo isn't wrong, sloppy, or false; it simply doesn't belong to the matter at hand.
Extraneous marks that outsider status — imported material a subject never asked for.
Extraneous and superfluous — a unit-mate — divide the territory of 'too much.' Extraneous material comes from outside the subject: the pet timeline on a volcano poster.
Superfluous material belongs in kind but exceeds the need: the fourth example proving a point the first three settled.
Off-topic, reach for extraneous; on-topic but past need, superfluous.

The conservator's first task with the harbor painting was subtraction.
Under ultraviolet light, whole passages glowed a different age: a lighthouse, two gulls, and a band of dramatic cloud, none painted by the original artist.
A dealer had added them a century later to suit Victorian taste.
However pretty, they were extraneous — imported onto a canvas they were never part of.
The original varnish line ran beneath them, unbroken, like a floor under later furniture.
Solvent by solvent, the additions lifted away, and the painter's own bare, quiet harbor came back.
